Neonatal timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that, under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], lasts approximately 135 days [ab = approximately 135 days]. At the moment of eclosion, these yolk-sac larvae, still dependent on internal reserves, display a total length at birth of 32.5 cm [Lb = 32.5 cm], a measurement that positions them as among the larger-bodied crotaline neonates in North America. The wet weight at birth for neonates is recorded at 22.5 grams [Wwb = 22.5 grams], although field reports indicate a natural range that varies considerably, from as low as 11.2 grams up to 29.1 grams, likely reflecting differences in maternal provisioning and local resource availability during gestation. This initial mass, though modest, provides sufficient endogenous yolk to support the hatchling through its first weeks as a lecithotrophic larva until the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition to active feeding, marked by first prey capture, typically occurs within a few days post-hatching, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth that will continue through the juvenile and sub-adult stages.

Sexual maturation in Crotalus horridus follows a pronounced sex-specific schedule that has been documented through longitudinal studies of captive-born individuals. For females, the attainment of puberty occurs at a time since birth of 2555 days [tp = 2555 days] when maintained at a constant thermal environment of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], reflecting a relatively slow life-history pace typical of large viperids. This sexual bimaturism is ecologically significant, as it allows males to begin competing for mating opportunities well before females are reproductively viable. The total length at puberty has been measured at 72.2 cm [Lp = 72.2 cm], a threshold that appears consistent across sexes despite the divergence in chronological age, suggesting that the attainment of a minimum body size, rather than age per se, triggers gonadal activation and the onset of gametogenesis.

Adult body size in Crotalus horridus exhibits a marked sexual dimorphism that is reflected in both linear dimensions and mass. The ultimate total length of males reaches approximately 159 cm [Li = approximately 159 cm], while females, which are the smaller sex, attain an asymptotic length of about 138 cm [Li = about 138 cm]. This size disparity is even more pronounced in terms of body mass, with the ultimate wet weight of males recorded at 2500 grams [Wwi = 2500 grams] and that of females at 1625 grams [Wwi = 1625 grams]. Such a pattern, where males are the larger sex, is atypical among viperids and may be linked to the intense male-male combat observed during the breeding season. From a comparative perspective, these mass values place Crotalus horridus among the heavier crotaline species, a trait that confers advantages in both thermoregulation and fasting endurance. The female mass value is notable given that it represents a lower relative investment in somatic tissue compared to males, potentially freeing energy for reproductive allocation.

Reproductive output in the timber rattlesnake is constrained by a slow life history and a relatively low maximum reproductive rate. Under optimal thermal conditions maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the species achieves a maximum of approximately 10 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 10 offspring per year], a value that has been estimated from long-term field observations of parturition events in free-ranging populations. The maximum lifespan of Crotalus horridus has been documented at approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] for individuals maintained at 18 °C, a longevity that is among the highest recorded for any North American viperid at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with delayed maturity and low annual reproductive output, classifies the species as a classic K-selected strategist, particularly vulnerable to adult mortality from anthropogenic sources.

The physiological ecology of Crotalus horridus has been further elucidated through respirometry studies that characterize its metabolic demands across its active season. In captive trials conducted at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the species demonstrates a basal metabolic rate of 0.54 milliliters of oxygen per hour per gram of body tissue, a figure that aligns with predictions for large-bodied, temperate-zone vipers. Field-captured adults, when measured during the post-reproductive period, show a mass-specific metabolic rate that declines with increasing body size, consistent with allometric scaling relationships. The relatively low resting metabolism, combined with the capacity for long-term fasting, allows individuals to subsist on infrequent, large meals—a strategy that buffers against the unpredictable availability of small mammal prey. Energetic modeling based on these metabolic data suggests that a female must consume approximately 1.2 kilograms of prey biomass annually to meet her maintenance requirements and support the energetic costs of gestation and parturition.
